items.prompt: A commercial application requires a specific MySQL-compatible engine, stored procedures, and managed backups. Which selection step comes first?
constraints: The application is a managed relational candidate.

options.text: Confirm the exact RDS or Aurora engine and version compatibility, then size instance, storage, connections, backup, and failover from measured workload requirements.
Choose any relational engine because SQL syntax is identical across vendors.
Choose a NoSQL service and preserve stored procedures unchanged.
Choose the newest engine version without application testing.

feedback.Reason: Engine compatibility and version behavior are part of the application contract before performance sizing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS and Aurora engines differ in SQL features, extensions, drivers, versions, and operational behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect tests the application on the selected engine and then sizes compute, storage, connections, and replicas.
Details.errorCorrection: SQL is not fully identical, NoSQL does not preserve relational procedures, and latest versions can break compatibility.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Engine compatibility may constrain feature choices while managed operations reduce undifferentiated work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SQL dialects, extensions, and engine behavior differ.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: NoSQL requires a different data and application model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Version upgrades need compatibility and performance testing.

items.prompt: A relational workload needs one writer, multiple read endpoints, and fast reader failover. Which Aurora structure should be evaluated?
constraints: The application can use cluster endpoints.

options.text: Evaluate an Aurora cluster with writer and reader instances or endpoints, sizing instance classes, replicas, connections, and failover behavior.
Use one instance and direct all reads to the writer to obtain reader scale.
Use an S3 bucket as a relational read replica.
Use a cache as the only read source for data that must be current.

feedback.Reason: Aurora separates writer and reader roles and exposes endpoints for failover and read distribution.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Aurora cluster endpoints route to writer or reader instances according to role and failover state.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner uses the writer for mutations, reader endpoint for eligible reads, and tests promotion and connection refresh.
Details.errorCorrection: One writer cannot scale reads independently, S3 is not a relational replica, and stale cache data may violate correctness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Reader replicas add cost and replication lag and do not replace write capacity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Directing all reads to the writer preserves a read bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Object storage is not a database replica.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Caching requires freshness and invalidation policy.

items.prompt: A relational API has unpredictable demand and long idle periods but requires SQL and can tolerate scale transition behavior. Which option should be compared?
constraints: The application can handle connection and capacity transitions.

options.text: Evaluate Aurora Serverless or another managed relational capacity model, checking engine support, scaling latency, min or max capacity, connections, and cost.
Use provisioned maximum capacity all day without idle-cost analysis.
Use Lambda as the relational database and store state in memory.
Use a cache because SQL semantics are not needed during idle periods.

feedback.Reason: Variable SQL workloads can justify a serverless relational capacity model when its scaling and engine behavior fit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Aurora Serverless capacity adjusts within configured bounds and has version, connection, and scaling characteristics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect models warm capacity, scale transitions, query latency, connection pooling, and cost across idle and peak periods.
Details.errorCorrection: Provisioned maximum can waste idle cost, Lambda is not a database, and a cache does not provide SQL durability.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Elastic capacity may introduce scaling latency or feature constraints that provisioned instances avoid.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A maximum provisioned fleet can be wasteful for long idle periods.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lambda execution state is ephemeral and not a relational engine.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache cannot replace database semantics.

items.prompt: An RDS workload is storage-latency bound and needs predictable IOPS independent of capacity. Which configuration should be evaluated?
constraints: Capacity and IOPS have different growth curves.
The engine supports the storage option.

options.text: Evaluate an appropriate provisioned-IOPS storage configuration, sizing IOPS, throughput, capacity, instance bandwidth, and cost from the workload.
Increase database capacity only because capacity always determines IOPS.
Use local instance store as RDS database storage.
Increase connections to compensate for storage latency.

feedback.Reason: RDS storage selection separates capacity and performance dimensions when the engine and workload require it.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS storage types expose different relationships between allocated size, IOPS, throughput, and instance limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks reads and writes, verifies engine support, and monitors storage queue and database latency.
Details.errorCorrection: Capacity is not always IOPS, RDS does not expose instance store, and more connections can worsen I/O contention.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Provisioned performance costs more and remains bounded by instance and service limits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Capacity-performance coupling depends on storage type.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: RDS manages supported durable storage rather than customer instance store.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: More connections can increase contention and latency.

items.prompt: An RDS database needs automated failover for an AZ failure, while read scaling is a separate requirement. Which feature should be evaluated?
constraints: Read scaling is not the same as standby.

options.text: Evaluate a Multi-AZ deployment for high availability and failover, and separately evaluate read replicas or Aurora readers for read scaling.
Use a read replica as the only failover mechanism without validating promotion and application routing.
Use a cache replica as a durable database standby.
Place the primary and standby in the same AZ to reduce replication latency.

feedback.Reason: Multi-AZ standby and read replicas solve different availability and read-scaling objectives.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS Multi-AZ maintains a standby for failover, while read replicas serve read traffic and have replication behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect tests DNS or endpoint failover, application reconnection, and read-lag behavior separately.
Details.errorCorrection: Read replicas are not identical standby semantics, caches are not durable standbys, and same-AZ placement shares failure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: HA adds cost and may not improve read throughput; separate readers add more replication and routing complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Read replicas and Multi-AZ failover have distinct roles and guarantees.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A cache is not a database recovery copy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Same-AZ deployment does not isolate AZ failure.

items.prompt: A relational workload needs storage replication across multiple AZs with automated instance failover. Which Aurora property should be compared with standard RDS?
constraints: Read and write traffic are measured.

options.text: Compare Aurora's distributed storage and cluster failover model with the selected RDS engine's storage and Multi-AZ model against RTO, write, read, and cost requirements.
Assume Aurora and every RDS engine have identical storage and failover behavior.
Choose Aurora solely because its name guarantees lower latency for every query.
Use a read replica as a substitute for storage durability.

feedback.Reason: Aurora and standard RDS have different storage, cluster, replica, and failover architectures that need workload comparison.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Aurora separates a replicated cluster volume from compute instances and reader or writer endpoints.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect tests engine features, write durability, replica lag, promotion, and cost for the actual workload.
Details.errorCorrection: Managed relational options are not architecturally identical, product naming is not a latency guarantee, and read replicas do not replace durable storage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Aurora can improve recovery and read architecture but may constrain engine compatibility and add cluster cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: RDS engines and Aurora expose different storage and failover models.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Latency depends on query, instance, storage, and workload, not name alone.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Read replicas are derived copies, not the primary durable storage design.

items.prompt: An RDS workload has high lock waits and poor query performance after migration, while instance and storage capacity are adequate. What should be reviewed?
constraints: The engine and version are fixed.
Query and wait metrics are available.
Changes can be tested before production.

options.text: Review query plans, indexes, engine parameters, connection behavior, locks, and workload concurrency in a test environment before changing instance size.
Increase instance size without diagnosing locks or query plans.
Disable transaction isolation to remove all waits.
Add a read replica for a write lock bottleneck.

feedback.Reason: Database performance can be query, lock, or parameter bound even when infrastructure capacity is adequate.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS parameter groups, query plans, indexes, locks, and connection patterns affect engine execution independently of instance size.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner captures wait and plan evidence, tests a parameter or index change, and validates correctness and failover.
Details.errorCorrection: Blind scale-up may not fix locks, disabling isolation risks correctness, and read replicas do not remove writer contention.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tuning can improve performance without scale-up but requires engine expertise and regression testing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More compute does not automatically remove lock or plan inefficiency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Transaction isolation protects correctness and cannot be disabled casually.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Read replicas do not resolve writes and locks on the primary.

items.prompt: An RDS database spends most time in disk reads because its working set does not fit memory. What should be evaluated?
constraints: Storage is not the only bottleneck.

options.text: Evaluate a larger memory or appropriate instance class, then measure cache hit ratio, query latency, storage I/O, connections, and cost.
Increase storage capacity without changing the database working set or memory.
Add read replicas even though the same working set is cold on every reader.
Disable caching to force deterministic disk reads.

feedback.Reason: Memory capacity can reduce database I/O when the working set and engine cache are the bottleneck.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS instance classes provide different memory and CPU ratios; database cache effectiveness depends on working set and query pattern.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests a larger class and query tuning together and checks whether storage or CPU becomes the next limit.
Details.errorCorrection: Storage capacity does not increase memory, replicas may repeat cold reads, and disabling cache worsens I/O.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More memory costs more and may not help a workload dominated by scans or poor queries.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Capacity and memory are different dimensions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Read replicas scale reads but do not automatically solve a working-set or query problem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Database caching is a normal performance mechanism and should not be disabled blindly.

items.prompt: An RDS data volume grows unpredictably and a full disk would stop writes. Which feature should be considered?
constraints: The storage type supports the feature.
The workload can tolerate the modification behavior.

options.text: Evaluate storage autoscaling with a maximum threshold, free-space alarms, growth-rate monitoring, and a tested application and backup response.
Wait for storage exhaustion because RDS expands before writes fail in every case.
Delete old rows automatically without retention policy.
Increase read replica count to add primary storage capacity.

feedback.Reason: Storage autoscaling can provide headroom but needs bounds and monitoring because growth and service limits remain finite.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS storage autoscaling increases allocated storage based on thresholds within supported limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets maximum capacity, alarms before exhaustion, validates expansion and cost, and retains retention controls.
Details.errorCorrection: Full storage can stop writes, deletion needs approval, and read replicas do not add primary capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Automatic growth protects availability but can increase cost and does not reverse growth automatically.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Expansion is not instantaneous or unlimited and should not be left to failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Replicas add read capacity, not primary storage.

items.prompt: A parameter change is proposed for a production database and may require a reboot. What must be part of the plan?
constraints: The parameter has a documented apply type.
The database has an availability objective.

options.text: Check whether the parameter is dynamic or static, test it, schedule a controlled apply or failover, and validate query, latency, and recovery behavior.
Apply every parameter immediately because managed RDS never reboots.
Change the parameter on the writer without checking readers or failover.
Delete the parameter group to force defaults.

feedback.Reason: RDS parameter application semantics can affect availability and require a controlled change path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DB and cluster parameter groups contain dynamic and static settings with different apply and reboot behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner changes a tested parameter group, observes all instances or readers, and keeps rollback and maintenance evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Managed RDS can require reboot, readers may differ, and deleting the group is an uncontrolled configuration change.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A maintenance window may delay improvement but protects availability and diagnosis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Some parameters require reboot and are not immediately applied.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cluster and reader behavior must be considered as one database path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting configuration can cause unexpected defaults and outage.

items.prompt: A global application needs regional read latency and a disaster recovery copy, while writes remain in one primary Region. Which architecture should be evaluated?
constraints: Writes have a single authoritative Region.
Regional reads can be eventually consistent.

options.text: Evaluate Aurora Global Database or another cross-Region replication design, measuring replication lag, reader latency, failover, write routing, and recovery steps.
Use synchronous cross-Region transactions for every request without modeling latency.
Use a cache in each Region as the only database copy.
Use one primary Region and ignore remote-user latency.

feedback.Reason: Cross-Region Aurora patterns separate primary writes from regional read and recovery copies with explicit lag and failover trade-offs.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Aurora Global Database replicates storage across Regions and supports regional secondary clusters and promotion paths.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner defines write authority, read consistency, lag alarms, failover routing, and promotion rehearsal.
Details.errorCorrection: Synchronous cross-Region latency can violate user SLO, caches are not durable copies, and ignoring geography misses the requirement.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Regional reads improve latency but introduce replication lag and cross-Region recovery complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cross-Region synchronous coordination adds physical latency and availability coupling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Caches do not replace the authoritative database.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One Region may violate global latency and recovery objectives.

items.prompt: A database migration compares open-source and commercial RDS engines with different license terms and feature sets. What is part of the architecture decision?
constraints: The workload has a fixed performance target.

options.text: Compare engine features, extension compatibility, license cost, instance and storage performance, operational tooling, and migration effort against the workload.
Choose the cheaper license without testing feature or query compatibility.
Assume licensing is independent of instance size and replicas.
Choose a commercial engine solely because licensed software is always faster.

feedback.Reason: Engine economics and compatibility can dominate a database choice as much as raw performance.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS engine licensing, extensions, version support, instance usage, and migration behavior differ.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks queries, validates feature parity, and models total cost including replicas, storage, and operations.
Details.errorCorrection: License savings can be offset by rewrites, licensing can scale with capacity, and commercial does not guarantee speed.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A familiar or feature-rich engine may reduce migration work while increasing recurring license cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cheaper license can create functional and migration cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: License terms can depend on cores, instances, or deployment shape.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Engine price does not establish workload performance.

items.prompt: An RDS recovery test takes longer than the stated RTO because snapshot restore and database initialization were not measured. What should change?
constraints: Snapshots or backups are the recovery source.

options.text: Measure backup completion, restore duration, storage initialization, engine recovery, connection cutover, and application validation as one recovery path.
Assume a snapshot identifier equals an immediately ready database.
Increase read replicas in the primary Region to shorten restore time automatically.
Skip application validation because the database service reports available.

feedback.Reason: RDS recovery time includes infrastructure restore and application readiness, not just the existence of a backup.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Snapshots and backups require restore, engine startup, storage readiness, and endpoint or application reconnection.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner rehearses from a representative copy and records each step against RTO.
Details.errorCorrection: An identifier is not a ready service, replicas are not restore copies, and service availability does not prove application correctness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Faster recovery may require warm standby or more frequent copies and cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Read replicas do not automatically shorten a separate restore path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Application validation is part of recovery completion.

items.prompt: An RDS instance has low CPU but rejects new connections during traffic spikes. Which configuration area should be investigated?
constraints: The application creates many short-lived sessions.
A pooling or proxy option is available.

options.text: Measure database max connections, application pool size, connection lifetime, memory impact, and RDS Proxy or pooling suitability before increasing instance size.
Increase CPU only because connections are always a CPU limit.
Increase client retry count without a connection budget.
Create a new database connection for every request indefinitely.

feedback.Reason: Connection limits can be reached independently of CPU and require pool and proxy modeling.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Database connections consume memory and engine slots; RDS Proxy can multiplex client connections for supported patterns.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets bounded pools, validates proxy pinning and latency, and alarms on connections and rejects.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU scaling may not change connection slots, retries amplify attempts, and per-request connections create storms.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pooling reduces connection pressure but adds proxy cost and transaction or session-state considerations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Connection slots and memory are not equivalent to CPU.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unbounded connection creation is the cause of many connection storms.

items.prompt: An Aurora read-heavy workload has daily peaks and an unacceptable manual reader resize process. What should be evaluated?
constraints: Readers can be added or removed.

options.text: Evaluate Aurora read scaling or reader autoscaling from a validated metric, with minimum and maximum readers, lag, connection routing, and cost controlled.
Scale the writer for every read peak regardless of write load.
Add unlimited readers because readers have no storage or connection cost.
Use a cache without invalidation for transactional reads.

feedback.Reason: Aurora reader scaling can match variable read demand while preserving a separate writer path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Aurora reader endpoints and scaling policies can add capacity for eligible read workloads.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses a reader metric, configures bounds, validates lag and connection distribution, and measures cost.
Details.errorCorrection: Writer scale can overpay and does not create read replicas, readers have cost, and caches need freshness controls.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Reader elasticity improves peaks but adds replica startup and routing delay.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Writer capacity does not directly provide distributed read capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Readers consume instance, storage, connection, and replication resources.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Transactional reads cannot be cached without correctness policy.

items.prompt: An RDS deployment must use a customer-managed KMS key and maintain recovery operations. What performance and availability dependency should be documented?
constraints: Create, restore, and failover paths must work.

options.text: Validate KMS key permissions, key availability, backup and restore access, rotation procedure, and the effect of key denial on database operations.
Assume encryption is independent of database creation and recovery permissions.
Delete the key after creating the database because ciphertext remains readable without it.
Use S3 encryption settings as a substitute for RDS volume encryption.

feedback.Reason: A customer-managed encryption key becomes an operational dependency for RDS data and recovery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS uses KMS permissions and key state for encrypted storage, snapshots, restores, and related operations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests least-privilege role access, rotation, cross-account or cross-Region recovery, and key failure response.
Details.errorCorrection: Key permission can block operations, deleting a key can make data unrecoverable, and S3 settings do not encrypt RDS volumes.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Customer key control improves governance but adds permissions, availability, and recovery responsibilities.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Key access is part of create, restore, and operation paths.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting or disabling the key can make encrypted data inaccessible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Each service's encryption control protects its own data plane.

items.prompt: A maintenance operation is scheduled during the database's normal peak and causes latency spikes. What should change?
constraints: The service has a latency SLO.
A standby or failover path exists.

options.text: Schedule maintenance in a lower-risk window, validate Multi-AZ or failover behavior, communicate impact, and observe database and application latency.
Disable all maintenance to preserve performance indefinitely.
Run maintenance during the peak because more traffic hides the spike.
Add read replicas without changing maintenance timing or failover testing.

feedback.Reason: Managed maintenance still has a timing and failover impact that should align with the workload SLO.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS maintenance, patches, parameter changes, and failover can affect instance or connection behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner selects a window, tests client retry and endpoint behavior, and monitors latency through the operation.
Details.errorCorrection: Indefinite maintenance deferral creates security and support risk, peak maintenance worsens impact, and replicas do not remove the operation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A maintenance window may delay changes but reduces customer impact.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Security and engine maintenance cannot be deferred indefinitely.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Readers do not eliminate writer or cluster maintenance effects.

items.prompt: An application connects to a specific database instance endpoint and fails after failover. What configuration should be corrected?
constraints: The database has a failover endpoint.

options.text: Use the appropriate RDS or Aurora cluster endpoint, configure connection retries and DNS refresh, and test pool invalidation after failover.
Hard-code the writer instance IP address so it never changes.
Use a reader endpoint for writes to avoid promotion.
Disable failover because endpoint changes are inconvenient.

feedback.Reason: Managed database failover requires clients to use role-aware endpoints and recover stale connections.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS and Aurora endpoints abstract instance role and can resolve to a new writer or reader after failover.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner configures bounded retry, DNS and pool behavior, and validates transaction recovery and idempotency.
Details.errorCorrection: IPs and instance endpoints can become stale, reader endpoints are not write routes, and disabling failover sacrifices availability.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Reconnect handling can briefly delay requests but preserves failover capability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Reader endpoints are not a writer failover solution.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Endpoint behavior should be handled in the application rather than removing HA.

items.prompt: A design picks Aurora or RDS from an availability label but has not mapped engine, read, write, storage, connection, backup, or cost requirements. What is missing?
constraints: Failure and performance objectives are explicit.

options.text: Compare engine compatibility, transaction and query behavior, writer and reader topology, storage and IOPS, connections, backups, failover, scaling, cost, and operational ownership.
Choose Aurora for every relational workload because it is always faster.
Choose RDS from storage price alone without request or recovery modeling.
Choose the engine with the most replicas regardless of write or connection needs.

feedback.Reason: Aurora and RDS selection is a complete workload and operations decision, not a single availability or price attribute.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Engine, cluster, instance, storage, reader, connection, backup, and failover choices interact.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect profiles the application, chooses one canonical managed relational shape, and tests migration and recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: Aurora is not universally faster or compatible, storage price omits usage and recovery, and replica count does not solve every write path.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A specialized cluster model may improve scale or recovery while increasing feature and operational constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Workload fit and engine compatibility determine performance, not product name.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Storage price is one of many cost and recovery dimensions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Replica count cannot replace writer, connection, or transaction design.
